course.title: Atomic – Cambridge Lower Secondary Science — Stage 7

unit.title: Measurements
unit.blurb: Why scientists measure, SI units, and how to measure length, area, volume, mass and time accurately – avoiding parallax errors and outliers.

O1.t: Distinguish qualitative and quantitative observations and name SI units for physical quantities.

O2.t: Measure length with suitable instruments, convert units and avoid parallax error.

O3.t: Repeat measurements, spot outliers, calculate averages and explain accuracy and precision.

O4.t: Calculate area (base × height) and convert units of area.

O5.t: Measure volume with a measuring cylinder (meniscus) and by displacement; convert units of volume.

O6.t: Measure mass with a balance, using tare, and convert units of mass.

O7.t: Measure time intervals and convert units of time.

captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was created by Atomic Education to help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence. Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 2: Measurements.
Today we will learn why scientists measure things, which units they use, and how to measure length, area, volume, mass and time accurately.
How can a running track be exactly the same length all around the world?
And how do we measure the tiny differences in time that decide a world record, or the height of a high jump?
Measurements must be made in standard units. Otherwise we could never compare athletes from different countries, and there would be no world records.
Measurement also helps us look after our planet. Scientists measure air quality, water pollution and animal populations to protect the environment.
Look at this runner. How fast is she really running? How could we find out?
If we say “she runs fast”, we are making a qualitative observation. It is described in words.
If we measure that she runs 100 metres in 14.2 seconds, we are making a quantitative observation. It uses numbers.
We use instruments to make quantitative observations. That makes them objective: based on facts, not opinions.
Long ago, people measured with parts of their bodies. A cubit was the length from the elbow to the tip of the longest finger. But people's arms are not all the same size!
So people began to use sticks and pieces of string marked with standard lengths.
In 1875, scientists agreed to define the metre using a special bar made of a hard platinum and iridium alloy, which does not rust or scratch easily. It was kept locked away in Paris.
Today we use modern instruments, like tape measures, electronic balances, stopwatches and thermometers, to make accurate measurements.
Length is a physical quantity: something in the physical world that can be measured. Mass, time and temperature are physical quantities too.
Scientists around the world have agreed on standard units for each quantity, called SI units. Length is measured in metres and mass in kilograms.
Time is measured in seconds, temperature in kelvin, and electric current in amperes.

sections.title: Measuring length

q.prompt: Clip readings 3.2, 3.0 and 26.8 cm. Average without the outlier?

stops.note: Paused after: “Here, the darts are close together but far from the centre: precise but not accurate.”

q.prompt: Close together but away from the target is…

captions: Length is the distance between two points. Height and diameter are lengths too. The SI unit of length is the metre.
For very large or very small lengths we use prefixes. Kilo means a thousand, so a kilometre is a thousand metres. Milli means one thousandth, so a millimetre is a thousandth of a metre.
To change a big unit into a smaller one, we multiply. To change a small unit into a bigger one, we divide.
So: one kilometre is 1000 metres, one metre is 100 centimetres, and one centimetre is 10 millimetres.
The instrument must match the job. We use a metre rule for longer lengths, like a piece of wood, and a 30 centimetre rule for small objects like a book or a pen.
A soft tape measure wraps around curved things like your waist. A hard tape measure is good for rooms and furniture.
Vernier calipers measure very small lengths, such as the width of a pin or the size of a bolt.
For big distances we use a measuring wheel for a sports field, an odometer for the distance a car travels, and a theodolite, which surveyors use to measure distances and angles.
To measure length with a rule, first line up one end of the object with the zero mark.
If you read the scale from an angle, from position A or C, you get the wrong reading: 19.8 or 20.2 centimetres.
Put your eye directly above the mark, at position B, and you read the correct value: 20.0 centimetres.
Reading from the wrong angle is called a parallax error. Always look vertically down at the mark.
How can you tell if a measurement is accurate? First, ask if it is reasonable. A paper clip 26.8 centimetres long? That can't be right, so measure again.
Always repeat measurements. Three measurements are enough if at least two of them are close together. Close results are precise.
Leave out any obviously wrong result, called an outlier, and calculate the average. For clip X, 3.2 plus 3.0, divided by 2, gives 3.1 centimetres.
If other people repeat the measurement and get the same results, our results are reliable.
Accuracy and precision are not the same. Here, every dart is close to the centre and close together: high accuracy and high precision.
Here, the darts are close together but far from the centre: precise but not accurate.
These darts are spread out. On the left they average near the centre, but on the right they are neither accurate nor precise.
Remember: accurate means close to the true value, and precise means close to one another. Darts that land close together but away from the target are precise, but not accurate.

captions: Area is the amount of space taken up by a flat, two-dimensional surface. The SI unit is the square metre.
This mosaic is made of small tiles, each 1 centimetre by 1 centimetre, so each has an area of 1 square centimetre. Ten rows of ten tiles make 100 tiles, so the area is 100 square centimetres.
A tile 12 centimetres long and 7 centimetres high has 12 times 7, which is 84 square centimetres. So for a rectangle, area equals base times height.
To convert units of area, square the length factor. Since 1 metre is 100 centimetres, 1 square metre is 100 times 100, which is 10,000 square centimetres.

sections.title: Volume

stops.note: Paused after: “One litre is a thousand millilitres, which is the same as a thousand cubic centimetres. So”
Paused after: “The curved surface is called the meniscus. For an accurate reading, read the level at the ”
Paused after: “Subtract: 49 minus 38 equals 11. The volume of the stone is 11 cubic centimetres, because ”

captions: Volume is the amount of space taken up by an object or a substance. The SI unit is the cubic metre, but a cubic metre is very big!
So we often use smaller units: the cubic centimetre, the litre and the millilitre.
One litre is a thousand millilitres, which is the same as a thousand cubic centimetres. So one millilitre equals one cubic centimetre.
We measure the volume of a liquid with a measuring cylinder. Look closely: the surface of the water curves up where it touches the glass.
If your eye is too high or too low, you will make a parallax error and read the wrong volume.
Put your eye level with the surface of the liquid.
The curved surface is called the meniscus. For an accurate reading, read the level at the bottom of the meniscus.
How do we find the volume of an irregular object, like a stone? We can't use a formula, so we use the displacement method.
First, pour some water into a measuring cylinder and record the starting volume: 38 cubic centimetres.
Then carefully lower the stone into the water on a string. The water level rises to 49 cubic centimetres.
Subtract: 49 minus 38 equals 11. The volume of the stone is 11 cubic centimetres, because it pushed aside its own volume of water.

captions: The mass of an object is the amount of matter in it. The SI unit is the kilogram.
Smaller masses are measured in grams and milligrams. One kilogram is 1000 grams, and one gram is 1000 milligrams.
A feather has a mass of only about 0.008 grams, while a cat has a mass of about 3 to 5 kilograms.
What about your suitcase at the airport? Its mass is measured in kilograms.
We measure mass with a balance. There are beam balances and electronic balances. Always start by setting the reading to zero.
Often we don't want to include the mass of the container. Put the empty beaker on the balance first.
Then press the tare button. The reading goes back to zero.
Now add the substance. The balance shows only the mass of the substance: 25 grams.

captions: The SI unit of time is the second. We also use minutes and hours: one hour is 60 minutes, and one minute is 60 seconds.
Over the centuries people have measured time in many ways, for example with sundials and hourglasses.
Today clocks, watches and smartphones keep track of the time of day.
To measure a time interval, such as how long an object takes to travel a distance, we use a stopwatch or a laboratory timer.
Now it is your turn to shine! Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.

Question 3: Water rises from 30 cm³ to 42 cm³ when a stone is added. What is the stone's volume? Pause the video now.
Answer: 42 − 30 = 12 cm³.
Question 4: Darts land close together but far from the target. Accurate or precise? Pause the video now.
Answer: Precise but not accurate.
